ne.headline: Niger energy ministry hosts students for open day
ne.dek: The Ministry of Energy organized an event in Niamey on October 22, 2026, for students to learn about energy sovereignty.
paragraphs: Niger's Ministry of Energy held an open day in Niamey on October 22, 2026, for students and pupils to discuss energy sovereignty. The event, themed "Energy Sovereignty: Challenges, Prospects, and the Contribution of Nigerian Youth," was part of World Energy Day celebrations. Students from the Scientific College and High School, the Military Prytanée, the School of Mines, Industry and Geology (EMIG), and the Abdou Moumouni University of Niamey attended.

Minister of Energy Colonel Seyni Alzouma praised the youth's engagement and thanked ministry staff for the event's success. He announced that the open day would be repeated in future years due to student interest. "We consider you ambassadors of energy from now on," Colonel Alzouma told the attendees, emphasizing the ministry's goal to provide reliable, low-cost electricity to the population. He highlighted the importance of renewable energy sources, which are cheaper than thermal options like coal, gasoil, or fuel oil.

During the open day, participants attended presentations on the energy sector, the ministry's structure, and the roles of various agencies. These included the National Agency for the Control of Interior Electrical Installations (CONTRELEC), the Nigerien Agency for the Promotion of Rural Electrification (ANPER), the National Solar Energy Agency (ANERSOL), the Nigerien Coal Company (SONICHAR), and the National Company for Mineral Coal Carbonization (SNCC-SA).

rw.headline: Rwanda coffee fetches record US$452 per kilogramme
rw.dek: K-Organics Ltd's specialty coffee sold for five times the previous year's price at the Best of Rwanda auction.
paragraphs: Rwanda's specialty coffee reached a record US$452 per kilogramme at the Best of Rwanda 2026 online auction on October 21. This price, equivalent to about Rwf670,000, was paid for coffee produced by K-Organics Ltd.

The winning bid was five times higher than the Rwf130,000 achieved by the company in 2025, and about 66 times the international market average of US$6.90 per kilogramme, according to the National Agricultural Export Development Board (NAEB). NAEB chief executive Claude Bizimana called the result a milestone for the country's coffee industry.

Bizimana attributed the record price to farmers' adoption of good agricultural practices, supply-chain contributions, and suitable coffee varieties. Farmers benefit from a 75% profit-sharing arrangement from coffee sales, with processing and exporting companies receiving the remaining 25%.

rw.headline: Rwanda begins month-long local elections
rw.dek: Voters will choose village leaders and representatives for district and national councils.
paragraphs: Rwanda's month-long local elections started on Saturday, October 24, 2026, with voters selecting village leaders and representatives for local councils. The voting process will continue through November 2026, ultimately electing new district leaders across the country.

The National Electoral Commission (NEC) has utilized social media, including the hashtag #Amatora2026, to inform voters and explain the electoral process. Official accounts from NEC and the Ministry of Local Government have shared reminders and graphics to encourage participation in choosing leaders who will serve five-year terms.

The election campaign has focused on voter participation and civic responsibility, with officials urging residents to vote early. Messages, some featuring Minister Dominique Habimana and musician Bruce Melodie, have been amplified by government accounts and local media to reach various groups, including youth and women.

rw.headline: Rwanda to host African Grand Prix in early 2030s
rw.dek: Formula 1 signed a 10-year agreement for a new circuit in Bugesera, south of Kigali.
paragraphs: Formula 1 will bring the African Grand Prix to Rwanda in the early 2030s, following a 10-year agreement. A purpose-built circuit is planned for Bugesera, approximately 40 kilometres south of Kigali. The Rwanda Development Board is overseeing a wider project for sports, tourism, and infrastructure development.

African Union Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf stated that the deal should help young Africans gain skills and find work in the global sports industry. He described the agreement as a milestone for African sport, noting that major international events can attract investment and tourism. Formula 1 says over 100 million people across Africa follow the sport, with nearly 60 percent of fans in key sub-Saharan markets under 35.

The race marks Formula 1’s return to Africa for the first time since the 1993 South African Grand Prix. The new venue is intended to host events throughout the year, not just race weekends. Youssouf said the initiative aligns with the African Union’s Agenda 2063 vision for an integrated Africa.

rw.headline: Rwanda partners with Asian firm to attract investment
rw.dek: Raffles Family Office will promote projects including aviation, tourism, and real estate to wealthy clients.
paragraphs: Rwanda has partnered with Asian wealth management firm Raffles Family Office to attract hundreds of millions of dollars in private investment for projects in aviation, tourism, real estate, and infrastructure. The agreement with the Rwanda Development Board (RDB), announced on October 22, 2026, aims to connect international investors with priority economic development projects.

Raffles Family Office will leverage its network of wealthy individuals and international investors to promote opportunities in Rwanda, including developments for the planned Formula 1 Grand Prix. rw.headline: Rwandans report lower satisfaction with public services
rw.dek: Security remains the highest-rated governance area in the 13th Rwanda Governance Scorecard released Thursday.
paragraphs: Satisfaction with public services in Rwanda declined to 68.48% in the past year, according to the 13th Rwanda Governance Scorecard released Thursday by the Rwanda Governance Board (RGB). Security and public order scored 90.15%, an increase from the previous year, making it the country's highest-rated governance area. The annual assessment, published Oct. 22, 2026, showed service delivery as the lowest of eight categories.

The scorecard assesses governance through 35 indicators, drawing on citizen surveys and administrative data. While overall national security satisfaction stood at 97.7%, personal and property safety declined by 3.32 points. Anti-corruption, transparency and accountability rose to 85.80%, and rule of law scored 85.47%.

RGB Chief Executive Dr. Doris Uwicyeza Picard stated that the findings should inform policy and public spending. Digital public services scored 60.98%, a decline from the previous assessment, with electronic court filing services at 65.40%. Agricultural services satisfaction was 53.70%.

paragraphs: Moto-taxis, the primary transport for people and goods in Sao Tome and Principe, resumed services on October 23, 2026, after a 15-day halt caused by a gasoline stock rupture.

Motorcycle taxi driver João Paulo de Moura reported resuming activities with significant debt from missed weekly payments, stating he owed 2,000 dobras. Taxi driver Cabral Lima noted October 22 was his 'day zero' for service, having used his car's fuel money for food.

Both taxi and moto-taxi drivers highlighted that the gasoline's return does not solve all issues, pointing to the urgent need for government formation following the September 27 legislative elections.

paragraphs: Gasoline and domestic kerosene are now on sale at filling stations across Sao Tome and Principe, ending a nearly two-week stockout of these products. Fuel became available on the morning of October 22, 2026, after a tanker discharged its cargo at the port in Lembá district on Wednesday night.

The sale of fuel resumed 24 hours after Gareth Guadalupe, the Minister of State for Economy and Finance, expressed regret over the shortages and their impact on the population. Guadalupe stated that over 50% of the cost of the recent import was for diesel, as a large part of the nation's energy matrix still relies on it.

Guadalupe also mentioned plans to mitigate the crisis by introducing 10 to 11 megawatts of solar energy by the end of the year and developing a factory to produce gas in Sao Tome and Principe for domestic use, transitioning away from petroleum.

st.headline: Project teaches 80% of Sao Tome and Principe to swim
st.dek: Rita Fernandes' "Sao Tome and Principe a Nadar" project trains local instructors and teaches swimming skills to islanders.
paragraphs: The "Sao Tome and Principe a Nadar" project is teaching islanders to swim, aiming to equip over 80% of the population with this life skill. Rita Fernandes, a former professional swimmer, founded the initiative three years ago after observing the lack of swimming proficiency in the island nation where fishing is a significant activity.

Fernandes, who has a background in Sociology and Sports Management, partnered with local teacher Angélico Santos, who had recently established the Sao Tome and Principe Swimming Federation. The project addresses the absence of public swimming pools and the lack of swimming in the official education system, despite children's proximity to the sea.

The initiative has evolved into a structured cooperation with local and Portuguese institutions, including the Portuguese Association of Swimming Technicians (APTN). Through donations and partnerships, the project has provided training materials and conducted online and in-person training sessions, even sending young swimmers like José Dias and Tiago Pires to Portugal for pool training.

paragraphs: Popular football matches, known as Navétanes, have been suspended across the Dakar region starting Monday, October 26, 2026. Governor Ousmane Kane issued an order on October 23, 2026, halting these widely followed neighborhood games and related activities until further notice.

No date has been set for the resumption of the Navétanes, leaving the duration of the suspension indefinite. The YOG are scheduled to take place from October 31 to November 13, 2026.

sn.headline: Senegal postpones budget review to October 27
sn.dek: The National Assembly delayed its review of the 2026 supplementary finance law, originally set for October 23.
paragraphs: The Senegalese National Assembly postponed its plenary session to examine the 2026 supplementary finance bill from October 23 to October 27 at 10 AM. This adjustment was announced via a press release from the Assembly's communication department. The proposed law, numbered 40/2026, allows the government to modify the state budget during the fiscal year if revenue or expenditure forecasts change.

The parliamentary group Takku Wallu Sénégal abstained from the vote on the 2026 supplementary finance bill in a previous plenary session. This supplementary budget allows for adjustments to state spending and revenue to new economic realities within parliamentary procedures.

In separate operations, the Fatick gendarmerie arrested 378 individuals attempting irregular emigration between October 20 and 22, 2026. Seized items included boats, outboard motors, and significant amounts of fuel. Investigations into these emigration attempts are ongoing.

Macron was expected in Dakar on October 30 and 31 for what would have been his first official visit since President Bassirou Diomaye Faye was elected.

The visit, which also included a stop in Abuja, Nigeria on October 28, was aimed at reviving France's relations in West Africa. Paris sought to relaunch its relations in West Africa with this planned visit. The cancellation comes as France grapples with significant internal social challenges.

sn.headline: Mamelodi Sundowns eliminated from CAF Champions League

paragraphs: Defending CAF Champions League champions Mamelodi Sundowns were eliminated from the 2026-2027 competition after a 1-1 draw with Angola's Wiliete SC on Friday. The match, held at Loftus Versfeld Stadium in Pretoria, was the second leg of the preliminary round.

After a 0-0 draw in the first leg in Angola, Mamelodi Sundowns needed a home win to continue defending their title. Tashreeq Matthews scored for the South African side in the 11th minute, but Angolan forward Mabululu equalized in the 49th minute. This result meant the aggregate score was 1-1.

Wiliete SC advances to the group stage on the away goals rule, while Mamelodi Sundowns exit the tournament in the second preliminary round. The Senegalese club had previously lost the first leg 0-2 in Dakar and needed a comeback to qualify for the group stage.

sl.headline: sierra leone journalists trained on Ebola preparedness
sl.dek: Health officials and media representatives met in Freetown to improve reporting during public health emergencies.
paragraphs: Journalists in Sierra Leone received training on emergency preparedness and responsible reporting on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, at the National Public Health Agency (NPHA) headquarters in Freetown. The NPHA, working with the Independent Media Commission (IMC), conducted the one-day session to enhance accurate reporting and cooperation during health crises.

NPHA Executive Director Professor Foday Sahr stated that Sierra Leone's preparedness is precautionary, with no current Ebola outbreak, following developments in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda. He reported that the country's overall Ebola preparedness score rose from 51 percent to 83 percent after an October 8 reassessment, with infection control capacity improving to 82 percent and safe burial preparedness reaching 73 percent.

The training aimed to prevent misinformation and improve media coverage of public health emergencies, with IMC Executive Secretary Khalil Kallon presenting guidelines informed by past outbreaks like COVID-19. Professor Sahr urged journalists to verify information and avoid sensationalism, while Kallon stressed professional ethics and protecting vulnerable individuals' privacy.

He reported that the country's overall Ebola preparedness score rose from 51 percent to 83 percent after an October 8 reassessment, with infection control capacity improving to 82 percent and safe burial preparedness reaching 73 percent.

The training aimed to prevent misinformation and improve media coverage of public health emergencies, with IMC Executive Secretary Khalil Kallon presenting guidelines informed by past outbreaks like COVID-19. Professor Sahr urged journalists to verify information and avoid sensationalism, while Kallon stressed professional ethics and protecting vulnerable individuals' privacy.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone charcoal burning causes deforestation
sl.dek: Environmental agency warns of economic tree destruction and greenhouse gas emissions from burning wood for fuel.
paragraphs: 65-year-old Pa Alimamy has burned charcoal for over two decades in Sierra Leone, a trade he says sustains his family and many others across the country. The demand for charcoal as a cooking fuel is high because only 36% of the population has electricity and just 15% have access to clean cooking.

The Environmental Protection Agency in Sierra Leone acknowledged the environmental hazards of charcoal production, noting that burners are now cutting down economic trees like orange and mango. Director Paul Lamin stated this practice leaves land treeless, exposed to climate change, and threatens food security.

Charcoal burning emits significant greenhouse gases, contributing to climate change and air pollution, according to experts. The Food and Agricultural Organization estimates traditional wood energy emits 2.4 GT of carbon dioxide equivalent annually, with Sub-Saharan Africa accounting for one-third of these emissions.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone vice presidents lack succession path
sl.dek: No vice president has ever been elected president in Sierra Leone, raising questions about the current officeholder's future.
paragraphs: Sierra Leone's Vice Presidency, constitutionally powerful, has historically served as a political cul-de-sac rather than a route to the presidency. Since independence, vice presidents have often been appointed to balance regional or ethnic considerations, appease party blocs, or neutralize rivals, rather than to cultivate ambition for higher office. This has meant most vice presidents lack a clear succession pathway and an independent political base.

Post-independence history shows vice presidents like Sorie Ibrahim Koroma and Francis Minah were powerful but not groomed for succession, with Minah facing execution after an alleged coup attempt. Solomon Ekuma Berewa, considered well-prepared, lost the 2007 presidential election, demonstrating that competence alone was insufficient. Victor Bockarie Foh's tenure was short and politically constrained, while Samuel Sam-Sumana's experience highlights the insecurity of proximity to power without presidential backing.

The current Vice President faces a sharp question: has the historical pattern already sealed their fate? The office's design and past outcomes suggest a challenging path for any vice president seeking to transition to the presidency, with electorates often opting for perceived change over continuity.

sl.headline: Female artisanal miners report sexual violence in Kono district
sl.dek: Women working in diamond and gold pits in Jaiama Nimikor describe a pattern of rape and harassment while seeking income in abandoned mining sites.
paragraphs: Female artisanal miners in the diamond-rich district of Kono, Sierra Leone, are reporting frequent incidents of rape and sexual harassment while working in abandoned pits. Janet, a 32-year-old miner, stated she was raped at age 15 while scavenging for gold and diamonds in Jaiama Nimikor, a site located 8 miles from Koidu. She reported the assault to her village head, but the perpetrator remained unidentified.

Another miner, 48-year-old Haja, said she was raped by a man in her village after starting gold mining to support her three children. Haja reported the incident to a camp master, who dismissed her claim by suggesting the attacker was her boyfriend. She subsequently fled to the village of Guitor due to the stigma and shame associated with the assault before eventually returning to her home.

These women turned to artisanal mining as a primary livelihood following the end of the civil war. Many miners report that their attempts to seek justice through local authorities have been ineffective. Janet and Haja continue to work in the sector to provide for their families despite the ongoing risks of violence.

so.headline: Somali official survives alleged Turkish drone strike
so.dek: Hassan Abdulkadir, a key strategist for Laftagaren's forces, escaped unharmed after his motorcycle was hit.
paragraphs: Hassan Abdulkadir, former internal security minister of Southwest State and a key figure in Laftagaren’s forces, survived an alleged Turkish drone strike on Wednesday night. The strike hit a motorcycle carrying two of Laftagaren’s fighters, killing them. Abdulkadir and another military figure, Mustafa Qoomaal, were unharmed in the attack in the Bay region.

It is unclear if the strike targeted Abdulkadir, who is considered the main strategist for Laftagaren’s guerrilla campaign. His forces recently recaptured towns including Qansah-dhere, Burhakabo, and Dinsor. This is the second air raid on a Somali opposition politician; General Mahad Abdirahman survived an F-16 strike on September 3.

Abdulkadir has been seen in towns recently retaken by Laftagaren’s forces. The federal government had previously launched an offensive in March that ousted the former regional president. Laftagaren’s forces continue to consolidate their control over the Bay region.

so.headline: Somali opposition challenges new constitution in court
so.dek: Sharif Sheikh Ahmed seeks to annul the controversial charter, with the Supreme Court awaiting the government's defense.
paragraphs: Somalia's Supreme Court has set Thursday as the deadline for the federal government to respond to a legal challenge against the nation's new constitution. Opposition leader Sharif Sheikh Ahmed filed the case seeking to annul the charter, which regional states and opposition figures deem unilateral. They argue it was drafted without broad consensus and approved in March without opposition members of parliament present.

President Hassan Sheikh has praised the new constitution as a new chapter for Somalia, but Puntland, Jubaland, and the opposition continue to recognize the 2012 draft constitution. This earlier text was developed through a broad-based agreement among all political stakeholders. The current legal battle is seen by many as a test of the Supreme Court's independence, a quality long questioned due to alleged executive influence on judicial decisions.

The federal government aims to win the case or at least delay the court proceedings. The opposition's legal action highlights a deep political division over the nation's foundational law, with differing interpretations of legitimacy and national recognition.

ss.headline: Yambio infant needs surgery after baboon attack
ss.dek: A three-month-old baby girl in Yambio suffered severe facial injuries from a baboon attack and requires specialized reconstructive surgery.
paragraphs: A three-month-old baby girl in Yambio, Western Equatoria State, is in stable condition after a baboon attack severely damaged her nose. Health officials stated the infant was brought to Yambio State Hospital on Thursday morning with injuries that left only small openings for breathing. Medical staff inserted a nasogastric tube to assist feeding while the child receives treatment.

The infant requires specialized reconstructive surgery to repair her damaged nasal tissue, a procedure unavailable at the local hospital due to a lack of expertise and facilities, according to Dr. Kinawo Richard of the Western Equatoria State Ministry of Health. The baboon, which belonged to a relative, reportedly left its feeding area and entered the house before attacking the child. The Director of wildlife in the state, Joseph Dau Deng, urged residents to stop keeping dangerous wild animals in residential areas, calling it illegal.

Brigadier Justin Waiwai, Western Equatoria State Police Commissioner, condemned the incident and stated the baboon's owner will be held accountable. Deng warned that such animals pose a significant risk to children and the community. The exact circumstances of the attack remain unclear.

ss.headline: Special Court rejects Riek Machar's video evidence request
ss.dek: The court ruled Machar's application to play video footage supporting his arguments was premature.
paragraphs: The Special Court in Juba rejected former First Vice President Riek Machar's request to present video footage during his trial on Friday, October 23, 2026. Presiding Judge Dr. James Alala Deng stated the application was premature as the proceedings had not yet reached the stage for considering such evidence. Machar, 74, had sought to play videos of senior government officials to support his defence.

Judge Deng explained that Machar should first focus on understanding and responding to the specific charges against him, as the court had not yet framed the charges. The lead prosecutor had also opposed the application, arguing it was too early for video evidence. The court adjourned the proceedings to October 26, 2026, for the examination of the fifth accused to continue.

Separately, the Special Court announced it had completed an investigation into alleged threats against Machar, his defence team, and co-accused. Judge Deng said individuals identified in the investigation have been referred to the attorney general and police for further action. The defence team had raised concerns about the safety of the accused and their lawyers last month.

ss.headline: GIZ gives 12 grinding machines to South Sudan farmers
ss.dek: The German agency aims to boost income and reduce processing time for cereal farmers in Yei River and Magwi counties.
paragraphs: The Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH provided 12 cereal grinding machines to 12 farmer groups in Yei River and Magwi counties on Tuesday. Each group, comprising 25 members with 60 percent females, received one machine through GIZ's Improved Living Conditions and Psychosocial Support (ILiPS) project.

GIZ South Sudan stated the initiative aims to support income-generating activities by improving access to processing equipment, reducing time and effort for cereal processing, and increasing product value. Ramson Duku, Agricultural Advisor, emphasized the equipment's role in promoting self-reliance and strengthening household livelihoods.

The project will offer follow-up training and technical support to ensure sustainable use of the machinery, which is part of broader efforts to strengthen agricultural extension services and promote climate-smart farming. The ILiPS project also supports returnees, internally displaced persons, and host communities.

ss.headline: South Sudan shortens school year for elections
ss.dek: Primary and secondary examinations moved to November to allow for December 22, 2026 general elections.
paragraphs: South Sudan has reduced its academic calendar by one month to ensure national examinations conclude before the general elections on December 22, 2026. The Council of Ministers approved changes to the education schedule in September, advancing primary and secondary exams to November.

Hussein Abdelbagi Akol, the Presidential Advisor on Foreign Affairs and International Relations, and former Minister of Cabinet Affairs Dr Martin Elia Lomuro are among political leaders whose parties have joined newly registered coalitions. The Political Parties Council announced the registration of several political alliances on Wednesday as parties organize for the upcoming vote.

Dr Lomuro's South Sudan Democratic Forum is part of the National Agenda Coalition of Political Parties, which includes 10 political parties. Abdelbagi leads the South Sudan Patriotic Movement under the South Sudan Opposition Alliance. Two other coalitions, the Coalition of National Alliance of Political Parties and the National Alliance of Political Parties, have also been registered.

sd.headline: Sudan aid cuts worsen hunger, malnutrition
sd.dek: World Food Programme cuts and crop failure leave families struggling for food as prices soar in Darfur.
paragraphs: Displaced families and vulnerable communities across Sudan are facing a deepening hunger crisis due to cuts in food aid and widespread crop failure. The World Food Programme (WFP) has reduced assistance, while East Darfur has experienced a near-total crop failure, leaving households without food and income. Residents in Sheairia report soaring prices, worsening malnutrition, and shortages of essential medicines and therapeutic food for children.

Carl Skau, the WFP's acting executive director, stated the agency has the capacity to help millions but is running out of money. The General Coordination for Displaced People and Refugees warns that reduced aid could force families to skip meals and sell possessions. Spokesperson Adam Rijal said funding shortages threaten essential meals and could lead to desperate measures like withdrawing children from school.

Farmers in East Darfur harvested almost nothing of their main crops, including groundnuts and millet, leading to food insecurity. A sack of millet now costs around SDG 350,000, with prices for onions, cooking oil, and sugar also significantly high. Pregnant women struggle to get adequate diets, and children suffer from malnutrition, with limited supplies of therapeutic food available.

Youssouf urged all parties to protect civilians and humanitarian personnel, and ensure unhindered humanitarian access. He also stressed the need to respect Sudan’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

sd.headline: Khartoum denies drone strike role in Abyei market attack
sd.dek: Sudan's government rejected accusations of involvement in an October 19 drone strike that killed at least 153 people in Abyei.
paragraphs: Khartoum has denied its armed forces carried out a drone strike on Amiet Common Market in the disputed Abyei region on October 19. Sudan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs stated on Thursday that the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) had no connection to the attack, which killed at least 153 people and wounded 19. South Sudanese officials, however, blamed Sudan’s military for the incident.

The ministry expressed condolences to the victims’ families and wished the wounded a speedy recovery, but provided no evidence to support its denial. The victims included Sudanese, South Sudanese, and foreign nationals. The attack has increased tensions between Sudan and South Sudan, leading South Sudan to summon Sudan’s ambassador to Juba.

Meanwhile, the RSF-aligned Government of Peace has called for an international investigation into the attack. Its foreign minister, Ammar Amoun Deldoum, told Radio Tamazuj on Thursday that a complaint was filed with the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for Sudan on October 19. Deldoum stated that a local committee was also established to gather information from traders and survivors.

sd.headline: Sudan lifts ban on 46 imports amid rising inflation
sd.dek: The Sudanese currency reached SDG 10,300 against the dollar as annual inflation hit 28.29%.
paragraphs: Sudan has lifted import restrictions on 46 goods as the dollar climbed to SDG 10,300 and annual inflation reached 28.29%. Sovereignty Council chairman Abdelfattah El Burhan cancelled a cabinet decision that had banned these imports, aiming to ease pressure on consumers struggling with soaring food prices.

Finance minister Jibril Ibrahim stated the decision considers consumer needs while protecting domestic producers. Traders reported an immediate price fall for some goods following the announcement. The National Importers’ Chamber welcomed the move but requested a clear cancellation of Resolution No. 74, which had imposed the ban and caused losses.

Foreign-exchange dealers reported the dollar rose to SDG 10,200 for buying and SDG 10,300 for selling on Thursday, an increase of SDG 100. Annual inflation rose to 28.29% in September from 26.14% in August, with food and drink prices up 36.81% annually.

tg.headline: Togo men urged to check for breast cancer signs
tg.dek: Less than one percent of breast cancers occur in men, but early detection is key for treatment.
paragraphs: Men in Togo are being urged to be aware of breast cancer symptoms, as the disease can affect them too. While October Rose campaigns focus on women, male breast cancer is rare, accounting for less than one percent of all cases. This rarity means men may not recognize signs like a lump or nipple changes, delaying diagnosis.

A lump or nodule near the nipple, nipple retraction, skin changes, or a swollen armpit can indicate breast cancer in men. These signs, though not always cancerous, warrant rapid medical evaluation. Men with a family history of breast cancer, genetic predispositions like BRCA mutations, or certain hormonal conditions face increased risk.

Consulting a health professional is important if any suspicious signs appear, regardless of age or perceived risk factors. Early diagnosis through clinical exams, mammography, or ultrasound, followed by biopsy, improves treatment outcomes for men affected by this uncommon but serious condition.

tg.headline: Togolese opposition plans Brussels meeting
tg.dek: Togolese democratic forces and diaspora groups will meet in Brussels from November 27 to 29, 2026.
paragraphs: Togolese opposition groups CODITOGO and FREEDOM-TOGO MLN announced a meeting in Brussels, Belgium, from November 27 to 29, 2026. The gathering aims to strengthen the unity of the Togolese opposition and foster a new dynamic for citizen-led action to rebuild democracy in Togo.

This initiative follows discussions at the International Forum of Montreal in August 2025 and takes into account the January 26, 2026, ruling by the ECOWAS Court of Justice. The Brussels Assises will focus on promoting collaboration among democratic opposition actors, establishing a strategic consultation framework, and creating a permanent body for decision-making and dispute resolution.

The stated goals include building a culture of collaboration based on mutual respect and collective responsibility. The meeting also seeks to define new strategies and strengthen the convergence of initiatives to unite democratic forces around a shared vision.

tg.headline: Togo gas transport to resume by October 27
tg.dek: West African Gas Pipeline Company completed valve replacements and will now dry the pipeline.
paragraphs: Gas transport on the Lomé lateral pipeline, suspended since October 12, is expected to resume by October 27. The West African Gas Pipeline Company (WAPCo) announced on October 20 that it had successfully replaced two valves without incident. The company is now proceeding with water evacuation, drying, and inspection of the 19-kilometer pipeline.

WAPCo stated that the replacement of the subsea valve and the station's inlet shut-off valve occurred between October 14 and 17. The next phase involves internal inspection using a magnetic flux leakage tool to assess the pipeline's condition before gas transport can safely restart. WAPCo acknowledged the temporary interruption's impact on Togo's electricity production.

The company expressed gratitude to the Togolese government, the Ministry of Mines and Energy, CEET, ContourGlobal Togo, and the public for their patience. The project aims to ensure the safety, reliability, and sustainable operation of the West African Gas Pipeline system.

tn.headline: Tunisia plans 8.2% rise in public sector wages for 2027
tn.dek: The government expects to spend 27.349 billion dinars on salaries, an increase from 25.267 billion dinars in 2026.
paragraphs: Tunisia's draft budget for 2027 allocates 27.349 billion dinars for public sector salaries, an 8.2% increase from the estimated 25.267 billion dinars in 2026. This spending represents 39.7% of the budget excluding debt repayment and 13.7% of the gross domestic product. The budget also plans for 32,557 new positions, with education and higher education receiving the largest share of new hires at 7,388 positions.

Education will receive the largest portion of the salary budget, with 8.220 billion dinars, or 30% of the total. The Ministry of Interior follows with 4.404 billion dinars (16%), then National Defense with 3.307 billion dinars (12%), and Health with 3.172 billion dinars (12%). The draft budget also includes provisions for regularizing the status of workers over 45 and holders of doctorates.

The government aims for a 3.1% growth rate in 2027, though some business leaders find the economic recovery support insufficient. Yassine Gouiaa, president of the National Organization of Entrepreneurs, stated that the 230 million dinars allocated for economic recovery is too small, especially given the current crisis and rising energy costs. He noted that previous financing lines for startups have not yet been implemented.

tn.headline: Tunisia court upholds state security plot sentences
tn.dek: The Court of Cassation confirmed prison terms ranging from three to 35 years for 21 accused in a state security plot case.
paragraphs: Tunisia's Court of Cassation upheld all appeals against judgments in the "plot against state security 2" case on Wednesday, October 21, 2026. The prison sentences, initially issued in February 2026 and ranging from three to 35 years, are now final. The Tunis Court of Appeal's criminal chamber, specializing in terrorism cases, had delivered its rulings on February 3, 2026.

Rached Ghannouchi, leader of the Ennahdha movement, and Kamel Bedoui received 20-year sentences, an increase from their first-instance judgments. Former security officials Mehrez Zouari and Abdelkrim Abidi were sentenced to seven years each, down from 12. Fathi Beldi and Samir Hannachi received 15 years apiece. Several defendants, including Nadia Akacha and Mouadh Ghannouchi, were sentenced to 35 years in absentia. Some sentences include five years of administrative surveillance post-release.

The case involves accusations of forming a group linked to terrorist offenses, inciting violence, and plotting against internal state security. Charges also included preparing to alter the state's form and recruiting for terrorist acts. The court also confirmed a two-year sentence for Abdelkrim Harouni in a separate corruption case, alongside sentences for businessman Mohamed Frikha and former oil company executives.

tn.headline: Tunisian electricity company restores website after security alert
tn.dek: Steg reactivated its online services after implementing fixes for a global PHP2Shell vulnerability.
paragraphs: Tunisia's electricity and gas company, Steg, has restored its official website and online services after a temporary shutdown. The company had proactively disabled its digital platform due to a reported global computer vulnerability. This measure aimed to protect Steg's information system from potential malicious exploitation of the security flaw.

Steg stated that after applying necessary patches and ensuring security conditions were met, the platform is operational again. However, access to the website and its digital services is currently restricted to users within Tunisia. The company had announced the temporary suspension on October 22, 2026, as a precautionary step.

The global vulnerability, identified as PHP2Shell, affects the widely used PHP programming language. Millions of exploitation attempts were reported after its disclosure on October 21 and 22, 2026. Other Tunisian public bodies, like the ATCT, also temporarily suspended their sites to protect user data and systems.

zm.headline: Hichilema urges COMESA to boost intra-regional trade
zm.dek: Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema challenged the 21-member bloc to move beyond commitments and adopt ambitious economic growth targets.
paragraphs: President Hakainde Hichilema urged the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) to move beyond commitments and adopt ambitious economic growth targets. Speaking at the 25th COMESA Heads of State and Government Summit, Hichilema called for practical steps to strengthen intra-regional trade, mobilize domestic capital, and invest collectively in production and value addition. He stated that COMESA, with nearly 700 million people, has significant opportunities in minerals and agricultural produce.

Mr. Hichilema, who is the new COMESA vice chairperson, said member states needed to be aggressive in growing their economies and overcome a reluctance to trade internally. He noted that while intra-COMESA transactions appear encouraging, more can be achieved by strengthening commercial relationships and supporting locally produced goods. The President emphasized that Africa must lead its own development, with other partners following.

He called for the removal of trade barriers, faster movement of goods, one-stop border posts, and harmonized policies to reduce the cost of doing business. Vice President Mutale Nalumango stated that President Hichilema’s election to the COMESA vice-chairmanship supports Zambia’s export-based Grow Zambia Agenda.

zm.headline: ZDA signs $122m copper deal with Rong Xing
zm.dek: The agreement aims to boost copper cathode production and create 700 jobs in Kalulushi.
paragraphs: The Zambia Development Agency (ZDA) signed an investment promotion and protection agreement with Rong Xing Investments for a US$122 million copper processing project in Kalulushi. The deal, signed yesterday, involves Rong Xing investing in a project that will process copper ore into high-grade copper cathodes and concentrates.

Rong Xing Investments, a Zambian subsidiary of Jin Xun operating in Kalulushi for 10 years, has already invested US$42 million and is currently investing US$30 million in plant III construction. ZDA director general Albert Halwampa stated the agreement strengthens investor confidence and Zambia's position as an attractive mining destination.

The expansion project will increase copper cathode production capacity from 5,500 tonnes to 10,000 tonnes annually, supporting the government's goal of three million tonnes of copper production. The investment has already created 506 jobs and will add 194 more, bringing the total workforce to 700.

eh.headline: US proposes Minurso mandate change
eh.dek: Washington wants to alter the UN mission's role in Western Sahara ahead of a vote.
paragraphs: Tensions rose in Western Sahara as the United States presented a draft resolution to the UN Security Council on October 22, 2026. The proposal aims to redefine the role of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (Minurso), which is tasked with organizing a referendum. The US wants to extend Minurso's mandate but with significant changes to its operations.

The pro-independence Sahrawi group, the Polisario Front, reacted swiftly to the US proposal, feeling targeted by the suggested reforms. The vote on the extension of Minurso's mandate is scheduled to take place at the UN headquarters in less than 10 days.

The proposed changes come as the UN Security Council prepares to vote on the future of Minurso. The Polisario Front has threatened to withdraw from discussions if the mission's mandate is altered in a way they deem unfavorable.

ls.headline: Lesotho elected chair of SADC security organ
ls.dek: Prime Minister Sam Matekane will lead the regional body's politics, defence, and security cooperation.
paragraphs: Lesotho has been elected the incoming chair of the Southern African Development Community’s Organ on Politics, Defence and Security Cooperation. Prime Minister Sam Matekane was elected to the position during a virtual summit on October 21, 2026, ending a deadlock with Angola. This appointment places Lesotho in a leadership role within the regional bloc's most influential security structure.

Foreign Affairs Minister Limpho Tau stated the appointment reflects the region's confidence in Lesotho's political stability, noting the country was removed from the SADC agenda in 2025 after years of monitoring its domestic instability. The Organ Troika will now include Lesotho, alongside Eswatini and Malawi.

The organ is responsible for supporting democratic governance, conflict prevention, and regional security cooperation. Lesotho's new role means it will directly engage in discussions on regional challenges such as the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and violent extremism in northern Mozambique.

ls.headline: Green City estate guards paid with food parcels
ls.dek: Lesotho residents guarding Green City Estate receive monthly food parcels for 12-hour shifts.
paragraphs: Residents of Ha Abia are guarding the Green City Estate for up to 12 hours daily in exchange for monthly food parcels, a practice condemned by Labour Minister Tšeliso Mokhosi and MP Thuso Makhalanyane. The residents patrol the estate, prevent livestock from entering, and stop unauthorised people from accessing the property. Green City director Mahesh Patel stated the arrangement is voluntary community policing, not employment.

The food parcels provided to 10 selected residents include 12.5kg of maize meal, 12.5kg of bread flour, two litres of cooking oil, 2kg of beans, and 10 cartons of 500ml milk. Some residents feel the groceries are inadequate compensation for their demanding duties and have expressed dissatisfaction. An attempt to negotiate cash payments resulted in an offer of M550 per month.

The estate management initially arranged for a heater in a guardroom but removed it after residents raised concerns about their compensation. The arrangement was facilitated through local chiefs who identified residents willing to monitor the vast development's boundaries at Ha Pena-Pena.

ls.headline: Law minister blamed for M80 million election fund misprocurement
ls.dek: Richard Ramoeletsi allegedly authorised irregular purchase of IEC headquarters using unspent election money.
paragraphs: Law and Justice Minister Richard Ramoeletsi is implicated in the irregular purchase of the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) headquarters for M80 million. The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) is questioning his role in authorising the acquisition using unspent funds from the 2023 Local Government Elections.

The Maseru West property purchase from Homestead Holdings was not budgeted for in the 2023/24 financial year, yet the IEC used election money. Auditor General Mathabo Makenete flagged the M80 million expenditure, noting the IEC’s failure to remit unspent allocations to the government’s Consolidated Fund by March 31, 2024.

IEC executives admitted to the PAC that the commission acted wrongly in diverting funds. Finance Manager Mokheseng Mofolo stated the purchase was approved by former Director of Elections Mpaiphele Maqutu via a memorandum and routing slip.

ls.headline: Activists sue Lesotho education minister over school fees
ls.dek: SECTION 2 argues barring learners from exams for parental debt violates their right to education.
paragraphs: Human rights activists, SECTION 2, have taken Education and Training Minister Professor Ntoi Rapapa to the Constitutional Court. They seek to prevent schools from barring learners from final examinations due to unpaid school or examination fees. SECTION 2 argues this practice punishes children for parental debts, violating their constitutional right to education.

SECTION 2 Coordinator Morapeli Roman Masoto stated in an affidavit that excluding learners over unpaid fees interferes with their right to education. The group is seeking urgent court orders against the practice. The central question is whether Lesotho law permits educational consequences for children based on their parents' debts.

Mr Masoto argues that the law does not permit such exclusions, deeming the practice unlawful and discriminatory based on socio-economic status. He cited Section 25 of the Constitution, which supports the progressive realisation of state policy principles, asserting that this does not make Chapter III rights unenforceable.

ls.headline: Lesotho minister urges innovation for jobs
ls.dek: Minister Nthati Moorosi called for research to become businesses and practical solutions for national challenges.
paragraphs: Lesotho must transform its science and innovation efforts into tangible businesses and jobs, according to Minister of Information, Communications, Science, Technology and Innovation Nthati Moorosi. Speaking at the third National Science, Technology and Innovation Week 2026, she urged the country to move beyond annual discussions and apply research to solve national problems and drive economic growth.

The event, held at the Lehakoe Recreation Centre, aims to promote the practical application of science, technology, and innovation (STI) to improve the lives of Basotho. Minister Moorosi stated that nations investing in knowledge and innovation are better positioned to industrialise and compete globally, emphasizing that Lesotho needs to become a producer of knowledge and solutions, not just a consumer of technology.

The government is strengthening policy frameworks, including the upcoming Research and Innovation Policy, to support this transition. This policy seeks to turn research into commercially viable products and services by fostering collaboration between universities, research institutions, entrepreneurs, investors, and industry, ensuring research benefits factories, farms, businesses, and communities.
